units: a notebook heads the list of recommended kit
the torch in use must have a red filter to spare the dark-adapted eye
the steady mount is described as the item people neglect most
an instrument that shakes gives no usable image
the optical instrument comes only fourth on the list
a cheap model is judged good enough to start with
two eyepieces of different magnifications are recommended
a star chart is needed to find your way among the stars
going out regularly counts for more than the quality of the kit
text: Fancy a look at the night sky without spending a fortune? Start with the short list. A notebook comes first, because what you jot down beats what you half remember. Next a torch with a red filter, which spares an eye already settled into the dark. Then the mount, the bit everyone neglects and the bit that decides everything: an instrument that shakes will show you nothing. The telescope itself turns up only fourth, and a modest one is plenty for a beginner. Take two eyepieces as well, one for sweeping across a wide patch, the other for pulling in a detail. Add a star chart at the end, on paper or on a screen, or you will wander from one point of light to the next and recognise none of them. The kit counts for less than the habit. Go out often, even briefly, and your eye will learn on its own to tell what moves from what stays put.

units: the turning part of the building stayed jammed on the opening night
the guests waited outside while the trouble lasted
two technicians went up to check the mechanism
a piece of metal was caught in the rotation rail
one technician pulled the obstruction out and the other greased the gearing
the structure began to swing round again with a low rumble
the crowd first took that noise for a storm
the man in charge of the site gave an unprepared speech
the papers revealed the next day that the obstruction came from the building works themselves
text: On the opening night the dome flatly refused to turn. Guests waited on the terrace, glass in hand, while two technicians climbed the inner ladder to look at the mechanism. Wedged in the circular rail they found a strip of metal, dropped there at some forgotten moment. One of them worked it loose with a screwdriver; the other greased the gearing. Half an hour on, the whole frame began to swing round again with a low rumble that the crowd took at first for thunder. The shutter opened on a clear sky, and the man in charge of the site, plainly relieved, made a short speech he had not prepared. What he left out reached the papers the next morning: the offending strip had come from the building works themselves, a bolt left behind by the fitters, and it had very nearly wrecked an evening two years in the making.

units: hands must be dry and free of jewellery before the work begins
a greasy smear draws the particles that scratch the surface
the work is done in a closed room to keep draughts out
the disc is rinsed under lukewarm water with no cloth at all
fabric shifts the grains instead of carrying them off
every grain shifted digs a furrow that scatters the light of the stars
the water must drain off by itself before the rim is dried
repeated washing wears the reflecting film faster than the surrounding air does
text: Before you lay a hand on the mirror, dry it well and take off every ring you wear. The faintest smear of grease draws in dust, and dust will score the surface at the first rub. Set the piece down flat in a closed room, since one draught brings back onto the glass everything you have just cleared away. Rinse the disc under lukewarm water and use no cloth at all: fabric pushes the grains along instead of carrying them off, and each grain you shift leaves a small furrow that will scatter the light of the stars. Let the water drain away by itself, then blot the rim dry with a sheet of soft paper. If marks still remain, do not go at it again the following day. Wait a whole season, because washing too often wears out the thin reflecting film far quicker than a year of open air ever would.

units: the manoeuvres flown to avoid a collision are multiplying
the cause lies in the build-up of debris in low orbit
a tiny fragment can pierce a reinforced wall because of its speed
each impact breeds fresh fragments whose course becomes unpredictable
the problem therefore keeps feeding itself
the first answer is to catalogue the objects by radar
the second obliges craft to carry a fuel reserve to bring them down at the end of the mission
the third answer, still at the trial stage, plans the capture of a bulky piece of debris
text: Satellite operators report a steady rise in the number of manoeuvres flown to dodge a collision. Behind it lies a growing crowd of debris in low orbit: spent rocket parts, bolts, flakes of paint, all travelling fast enough that a chip the size of a fingernail will punch through an armoured wall. Every impact breeds fresh fragments, whose paths in turn grow hard to predict, so the risk keeps feeding itself. Agencies are testing three answers. The first is to catalogue what is up there by radar, in order to see close approaches coming. The second obliges each craft to carry a fuel reserve so that they can be pushed back towards the atmosphere once their work is done. The third, still at the trial stage, sends a chaser to seize a bulky piece of wreckage with a net or a harpoon and drag it down.

units: two neighbouring circular hollows show opposite aspects
the older one has a softened rim that has almost gone
its floor is lined with fine particles stirred by later impacts
the more recent one has a sharp wall cut into terraces
a pointed relief still stands at the centre of the recent formation
no pale streak surrounds the older formation
faint rays reach far out around the recent formation
those rays come from the material thrown clear at the impact
low light hollows out a marked shadow on the recent formation only
both formations belong to the same natural satellite
text: Two neighbouring craters offer the observer opposite kinds of relief. The older one shows a rounded rim, worn almost flat by time, and a floor lined with fine dust that later impacts have stirred over and over again. The younger raises a sharp wall cut into a run of terraces, and a pointed peak still stands on its floor. The contrast goes further than the ground itself. Around the old basin no pale streak survives; around the young one a web of faint rays stretches out a great distance, the mark of material thrown clear at the moment of the blow. Grazing light widens the gap again: the older hollow drowns in a single flat tone, while its neighbour cuts a hard, drawn-out shadow. One and the same natural satellite therefore carries, side by side, two faces of very different ages.

units: the piece raises the question of switching signs off after midnight
the writer refuses to treat the subject from the point of view of sky watchers alone
a beam aimed at the ground costs less than a beam scattered about
steady artificial brightness harms the sleep of people living nearby
it also sends migrating birds off course
a generation is reaching adulthood without having seen the milky band of our galaxy
the writer sees in that loss the end of a landmark shared by all humanity
not one of the points raised calls for complete darkness
the conclusion argues for aimed lighting, dimmed at night, and for protected areas
text: Should lit signs go off after midnight? The question deserves more than one angle, and it should not be left to those who watch the sky. Take the cost first: light aimed at the ground burns less than a beam scattered upwards. Take health next, since steady artificial brightness disturbs the sleep of people living nearby and sends migrating birds off course. Take, last, the point that looks weakest of all, the cultural one: a whole generation is reaching adulthood without ever having seen the milky band of our galaxy, and a landmark shared by all humanity is quietly lost. Not one of these points calls for complete darkness. Together they argue for lighting that is sparing, aimed downwards, dimmed after a certain hour, and for protected stretches of country where the sky stays black.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: she came into the optical workshop as a cleaner

she polished that disc through a whole night
the foreman examined the surface and put her on the bench

the delicate orders were kept for her
she passed on to two apprentices the rule never to force the glass
her last mirror is still in use and the team using it does not know who she was
text: She came into the optical workshop as a cleaner, very young, with no qualification behind her and nobody to speak for her. The foreman handed her buckets and sawdust, and nothing more. One evening she took up on her own a glass disc that an apprentice had spoiled, and she polished it until daybreak. The next morning the foreman held the surface up to a lamp, studied it, then put her on the bench. She never left it again. She learned to feel under her thumb a dip that no instrument of the day could measure, and the most delicate orders ended up at her place. Towards the end she trained two apprentices, repeating a single rule to them: never force the glass. The last mirror she polished still serves under a dome in the hills, and the team using it has no idea who she was.

units: the show traces the birth of a star and then its end
the images are judged unusually sharp
that quality comes from the scanning of genuine archive plates
the pace never slackens at any point
the lack of pauses ends up blunting the wonder of the audience
the unbroken music adds a needless weight of emphasis
the commentary explains too much and leaves nothing to imagine
the reviewer holds that a shorter show would have stayed with people longer
text: The show impresses, and that in the end is what undoes it. The seats tilt back, the vault lights up above you, and in one sitting you watch a star take shape, swell, and then collapse. The images have a sharpness you rarely meet, because the team scanned genuine archive plates one by one before setting them in motion. But the pace never slackens for a moment, and that want of breath produces the opposite of what was wanted: after a run of cosmic disasters, the viewer in the seat simply stops being amazed. The music, unbroken as well, adds a weight of emphasis the subject never needed. The commentary, for its part, explains far too much and leaves nothing to be guessed at. A shorter sitting, broken by silences and by a sky held still, would surely have stayed with people far longer.

units: the letter arrived the day before the sun was covered over
the person written to says he is giving up on watching
he pleads the want of an instrument and the want of nerve
the writer suggests pricking a sheet of card with a needle
the card held above a page throws an image shaped like a crescent
that method rules out any risk to the sight
a pale ring may close around the disc if cloud comes over
having no instrument invites you to watch the ground, the birds and the temperature
the writer asks for an account of what was felt
text: Your letter reached me the day before the eclipse, and I read it standing in the cold. You tell me you are giving up on watching, having neither an instrument nor the nerve for it. Let me put something else to you. Take a sheet of card, prick it with a needle, hold it at arm's length above a white page: the sun will draw a crescent there of its own accord, thinning as you watch, and your sight will be in no danger. If cloud comes over, do not go indoors. A pale ring may then close around the disc, and that circle alone is worth the walk out. As for having no instrument, it obliges you to look about you rather than up: the colour of the ground shifts, the birds go quiet, the air turns cold in a moment. None of that calls for equipment, or for any outlay. Write and tell me afterwards what you felt, and not what you thought you ought to feel.

units: the question concerns the difference between two rings seen around a heavenly body
the distinction lies in the matter crossed and in the optics at work
the first ring forms in high cloud made of ice crystals
those crystals bend the light through a fixed angle
the ring obtained is wide, whitish and steady in size
the second ring forms in low cloud full of droplets or in a veil of particles
it comes from diffraction and not from bending
that ring is narrow, coloured and pressed against the disc
its width varies with the size of the particles
a wide pale ring points to ice, a tight iridescent ring points to droplets or grains
text: A reader asks us how a halo differs from a corona, given that both of them wrap the body in a ring. The answer lies in the matter the light crosses and in the optics at work. A halo forms in very high cloud made of ice crystals with six faces, which bend the rays through a fixed angle; the circle you end up with is wide, whitish, and much the same size from one occasion to the next. A corona forms instead in low cloud loaded with droplets, or in a thin veil of fine dust, and it comes of diffraction rather than bending: that ring is narrow, coloured, pressed close against the disc, and its width follows the size of the particles. So keep one simple practical test in mind. A broad pale ring points to ice; a tight ring shot through with colour points to droplets or to small grains.
